title: Why Is the Bottom of Every Ship Painted Red?
hook: Why is the bottom of every ship painted red?
loop: Final line ends on 'the next time a ship is lifted out of the water,' which hands straight back into scene 2, 'Pull any ship out of the water...'. Pattern A: completed thought.

scenes.text: Can you believe this?
Pull any ship out of the water, and the bottom is always the same colour.
Red. Never blue, never green.
Is it simply tradition, copied from yard to yard without anyone asking why?
Actually, no.
Below the waterline, bare steel is a free surface for barnacles and weed.
They begin settling within weeks of a ship entering the water.
On a warm, shallow coast, a clean hull can disappear under a crust of living things in a single month.
A hull covered in growth is no longer smooth.
It drags through the water, and drag has to be paid for in fuel.
A heavily fouled hull can raise fuel use by as much as forty percent.
On a large container ship, that is thousands of dollars burned every single day.
So the coating below the waterline is not really paint. It is a slow poison.
It carries copper compounds that stop anything from taking hold.
Sailors worked this out centuries ago, nailing sheets of copper straight onto wooden hulls.
But the copper only works if it leaves the surface slowly.
Release it too quickly, and the protection is gone within a single season.
Release it too slowly, and the barnacles take hold anyway.
So the coating is built to wear away a few microns at a time, staying fresh for years.
